title: The Fore Highlands
text: Our story begins in the 1950s, in the eastern highlands of Papua New Guinea.
nxt: The Fore people lived there, in remote mountain valleys that outsiders had barely reached. A baffling illness was taking their lives.

title: The Laughing Death
text: The Fore called it kuru, a word that means shaking or trembling. Outsiders later gave it a darker nickname: the laughing death.
nxt: Patients first became unsteady on their feet. Then came tremors, slurred speech, and sudden bursts of laughter they could not control.

title: Zigas and Gajdusek
text: In 1957, a medical officer named Vincent Zigas reported the strange disease to a young American physician, Carleton Gajdusek.
nxt: Together, they started asking the obvious question. What kind of illness was this? It did not look like influenza, malaria, or any known infection. There was no fever.

title: A Bent Key
text: Here is how it works. Your brain makes a normal protein called PrP, which folds into a specific shape. A prion is the same protein, folded the wrong way.
nxt: Imagine a key that has been bent. The strange part is that a misfolded protein can push a normal one into the same bent shape. And then that one bends the next.

title: What Kuru Taught Us
text: Kuru showed medicine that an infection can be carried by a protein alone. It led to a Nobel Prize for Gajdusek and, later, one for Prusiner.
nxt: And it helped scientists understand diseases like mad cow disease and other prion disorders, which are still deadly today.

title: The Shudder
text: So the next time you meet cannibalism in a horror film or an old myth, remember that the scariest part may not be the monster.
nxt: It may be something far smaller: a single misfolded protein, patient and invisible, bending its neighbors one by one.
